title: DeepSeek-R1: reward right answers, not how to think, and reasoning emerges from training
summary: DeepSeek skips supervised fine-tuning and runs large-scale reinforcement learning directly on a pretrained model, with rewards based only on whether the answer is correct. The model learns on its own to think longer, reflect, and double-check. We take apart GRPO, work through the per-group advantage by hand, then examine R1's four-stage pipeline, its head-to-head with o1, distillation, cost—and the experiments that didn't work.
ai_summary: The DeepSeek-R1 paper (DeepSeek-AI; 2025; revised version published in Nature) applies GRPO to DeepSeek-V3-Base with no supervised fine-tuning, using rewards determined solely by rules for answer correctness and formatting. The resulting R1-Zero raises pass@1 on AIME 2024 from 15.6% to 77.9%, produces longer responses, and spontaneously develops reflection behaviors. The full R1 adds cold-start data, rejection-sampling fine-tuning, and a second round of RL, matching OpenAI o1 on math and competitive programming. Small models distilled from its 800,000 examples outperform same-size models trained with their own RL. Post-training cost is about $294,000.
brief: Problem: reasoning used to be taught with human-written demonstrations—expensive to label and capped by the quality of those demonstrations.
Method: skip supervised fine-tuning and run large-scale RL with GRPO. Rewards depend only on whether the final answer and format are correct, and GRPO replaces the value model with the group mean.

Result: R1-Zero's AIME score jumps from 15.6% to 77.9%, and it spontaneously learns to think longer and reflect. R1 matches o1 on math and competitive programming, and distilled small models stand out.
Limits: it depends on automatically verifiable tasks and a strong enough base model. Writing and similar tasks still need human data, and reward models are easy to game.

paper.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
paper.authors: DeepSeek-AI (core contributors include Daya Guo, Dejian Yang, Haowei Zhang, Junxiao Song, Peiyi Wang, and others)

cover.headline: A close reading of the DeepSeek-R1 paper
cover.highlight: Reward only the right answer, and reasoning grows on its own

sections.h: First, the conclusion: what this paper actually does

blocks.p: In January 2025, DeepSeek released the reasoning model DeepSeek-R1 together with this paper, which puts the model's training method into the open. In September of that year, a revised version of the paper was published in Nature after peer review. This article is based on the arXiv v2 update from January 2026, which includes the main text and dozens of pages of supplementary material.

The question it tackles is: **can a language model's reasoning ability be trained through reinforcement learning rather than being taught by hand?** Before this, the mainstream ways to make models reason were either to provide demonstrations in the prompt (chain-of-thought prompting) or to have the model imitate human-written step-by-step solutions. The paper argues that these approaches depend on large amounts of human annotation, and the model's ceiling is capped by the human-written examples.

DeepSeek's approach is surprisingly simple: take a pretrained large model (DeepSeek-V3-Base), **skip supervised fine-tuning**, and go straight to reinforcement learning. The problems are math, coding, science, and logic questions, and the reward looks at only two things: whether the final answer is correct and whether the format is correct. The reasoning process itself gets no constraints.

The result is a model called **DeepSeek-R1-Zero** that learned to "think longer" on its own: its responses became longer, and it began to double-check, go back and recalculate, try different approaches, and even write mid-solution, "Wait, here we can mark an aha moment." Its accuracy on the 2024 American Invitational Mathematics Examination (AIME) rose from 15.6% to 77.9%.

R1-Zero was hard to read and mixed Chinese and English. So the paper designed a four-stage pipeline to produce the final **DeepSeek-R1**: it is on par with OpenAI's o1 on math and programming contests, while also being able to write and answer questions. Finally, the paper used data generated by R1 to "distill" smaller models, and a 1.5-billion-parameter small model beat GPT-4o on math competition problems.

callout.title: One-sentence version
callout.text: R1 = a strong enough pretrained model + a batch of hard problems that can be graded automatically + large-scale reinforcement learning (the GRPO algorithm). No one teaches it how to think; the only reward is for thinking correctly. Long chain-of-thought, self-checking, and other reasoning behaviors emerge on their own.

callout.title: Four small concepts for reading this paper
callout.text: If you don't know them yet, these four are enough:
list: **Chain of thought (CoT)**: have the model write out intermediate reasoning steps before giving the answer.
**Reinforcement learning and PPO**: the model generates responses and adjusts itself according to their scores. PPO is the most common algorithm in RLHF. See the InstructGPT close read.
**KL penalty and reference model**: keep the model from drifting too far from what it originally was. See the DPO close read.

**pass@1**: the fraction of questions the model answers correctly when it gets one attempt per question. In the paper, each question is sampled multiple times, and average correctness is used as an estimate of pass@1.

sections.h: From DPO to R1: why return to reinforcement learning

blocks.p: The previous DPO close read told us: if the goal is to align with human preferences, you can skip reinforcement learning and simply classify a batch of existing good/bad answer data. But reasoning is different, for three reasons.

list: **No ready-made good answers**: the long reasoning processes we want were never written by anyone, or what humans wrote is not necessarily the best fit for the model to learn from. The paper argues that human-written solutions often omit reflection and checking.

**Correctness can be judged automatically**: math problems have standard answers, and coding problems can be run against tests. The reward does not have to come from human preference, nor from training a reward model to imitate people.

**It needs continual trial and error**: during training the model must keep generating new solution attempts and learn from its own successes and failures. Offline-only methods such as DPO cannot do this.

blocks.p: The paper's judgment is that the key to unlocking reasoning is not massive human annotation but three things: **hard enough problems, a reliable verifier, and enough reinforcement-learning compute**.
The RL algorithm R1 uses is called GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). It was proposed by the DeepSeek team in the 2024 DeepSeekMath paper to simplify PPO and save resources.

First, recall one pain point in PPO. Reinforcement learning needs to answer "how much better is this response than usual?" That "how much better" is called advantage. To estimate advantage, PPO trains an extra value model that predicts how much reward can be obtained from the current position onward. That value model is usually as large as the policy model and consumes a lot of memory and compute.

The paper points to a deeper problem: when the only reward is whether the final answer is correct, the value model is hard to train. This is especially true in long chain-of-thought: what the model wrote earlier may later be overturned by the model itself, and looking at a half-finished response makes it nearly impossible to predict whether the final answer will be right.

GRPO's solution: **for the same question, have the model produce a group of answers (say 16), and use the group's average score as the baseline**. Answers better than the average get positive advantage; answers worse than the average get negative advantage:

parts.desc: The reward of the i-th response. In R1-Zero this is the score for "correct answer + correct format."
How many responses are sampled per question. R1-Zero uses 16.
The mean and standard deviation of the group's rewards. Subtracting the mean compares each response with its peers; dividing by the standard deviation puts them on a common scale.

formula.note: No value model needed, and no human-written reference answer as a baseline: the peers on the same question are the baseline. That is also the meaning of "group relative" in the name.

plain.title: No coach, just compare within the group
plain.text: For the same question, have the model answer 8 times. Those 8 answers form a group. Correct answers get 1 point and wrong answers get 0, then each is compared with the group average: above-average answers are reinforced (green), and below-average answers are suppressed (red). PPO needs a value model to estimate "how many points this question should get"; GRPO uses the group's average instead, eliminating an entire model.

fig.title: Hand-calculating GRPO advantage: on hard problems, a rare correct answer gets the strongest reward; a rare wrong answer gets the strongest penalty
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: each question is sampled G = 8 times, correct = 1, wrong = 0; standard deviation uses population standard deviation. Numbers computed by this site from the paper's formula.
fig.note: On a hard problem, the one answer that happens to be correct gets strongly reinforced; on an easy problem, the one answer that happens to be wrong gets strongly suppressed. When every answer in a group is right or every answer is wrong, there is no difference within the group and the question provides no learning signal. Training problems therefore need to be at the right difficulty.

blocks.p: With the advantage in hand, GRPO's objective is very similar to PPO's:

parts.desc: The question and the i-th response.
The ratio of probabilities that the new model and the old model used at sampling assign to this response.
Clamps the probability ratio to a range so a single update cannot move too far. This is PPO's clipping trick.
The KL penalty, holding the model close to the reference model. In R1, β is only 0.001, so the leash is very loose.

plain.title: Don't change too much in one update, and don't drift too far from the teacher.
plain.text: There are two safeguards in each update. Clip limits how much the policy can change per step; even if a particular answer has a large advantage, the model only moves a small step toward it. The KL term ties the model near the reference, preventing it from producing weird outputs just to game the score.

blocks.p: The KL penalty also differs algorithmically from PPO. GRPO uses an unbiased estimator and puts it directly in the loss:

formula.expr: D_{KL}(π_{θ} ‖ π_{ref}) = π_{ref}(o | q) / π_{θ}(o | q) - log( π_{ref}(o | q) / π_{θ}(o | q) ) - 1

parts.desc: The ratio of the probabilities that the reference model and the current model assign to this response.
This expression is never negative, and equals 0 when x = 1 (the two models are identical); at x = 0.5 it is about 0.19, and at x = 2 it is about 0.31.

blocks.p: The paper explains why this choice matters for long reasoning. PPO splits the KL penalty into per-token pieces and treats it as part of the reward. Since reinforcement learning maximizes cumulative reward, longer responses accumulate more KL penalty, which **effectively punishes long responses** and discourages the model from "thinking longer." GRPO places the KL term in the loss, so this problem disappears. Also, training runs for thousands of steps and the model can drift far from the initial model, so R1 replaces the reference model with the latest policy model every 400 steps.

fig.title: PPO vs. GRPO
fig.subtitle: Compiled from Supplementary A.3 of the paper

For one question, take a group of rewards, subtract the mean, and divide by the standard deviation

blocks.p: To be fair, PPO can work. The paper compared the two on a 16-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model: with the common open-source default λ = 0.95, PPO was clearly worse than GRPO; after careful tuning to λ = 1.0, it came close to GRPO. The paper concludes that GRPO is not the only algorithm that can work, but it uses less resources and requires less hyperparameter tuning.

quiz.q: How does GRPO eliminate PPO's value model?
options: Replace the value model with a reward model
Sample a group of responses to the same question and use the group mean and standard deviation of rewards to compute each response's advantage
Train only with offline data
Set every response's reward to 1
quiz.why: The value model exists to provide a baseline of "what score is normal." GRPO lets a group of responses to the same question serve as each other's baseline: subtract the group mean and divide by the standard deviation to get advantage, so a value model as large as the policy model is no longer needed.

sections.h: R1-Zero: no instructions on how to think, only a reward for thinking right

blocks.p: R1-Zero's setup is extremely clean. The prompt template has only one requirement: first put the reasoning process between <think> and </think>, then put the answer between <answer> and </answer>. The paper intentionally constrains only the format and says nothing like "you should reflect" or "you should go step by step," so the team can observe what the model develops on its own.
**All rewards come from rules**, in two kinds with equal weight:

list: **Accuracy reward**: for math problems the model must put the final answer in the specified format (e.g. inside a box); a program compares it with the standard answer, giving 1 point if correct and 0 if wrong. For coding problems, a compiler and pre-prepared test cases determine correctness.
**Format reward**: whether the reasoning process appears inside <think> tags.

blocks.p: The paper **deliberately avoids neural reward models**, both outcome-only ones and process reward models that score each step. The reason: in large-scale RL, neural reward models are easily gamed (reward hacking), and retraining them costs extra compute and complicates the pipeline.

fig.title: Training problems used for RL
fig.subtitle: From Supplementary Table 4 and Section B.3.1 of the paper. All problems are in Chinese or English.
rows: Computational problems from regional contests to the International Mathematical Olympiad; no proofs
Comparison with standard answers (numbers, expressions, equations)
Problems similar to Codeforces and LeetCode; real issues from GitHub
Multiple-choice questions in physics, chemistry, and biology
Whether the chosen option is correct
Brain teasers, logic puzzles, 24 game, and reasoning questions adapted from coding problems
Writing, editing, QA, role-playing, etc. (used only in R1)
fig.note: Proof problems are excluded because it is hard to judge automatically whether a proof is correct. This also marks the boundary of the method: it depends on problems that can be verified automatically.

blocks.p: Training details (Section 2.1): learning rate 3 × 10^{-6}, KL coefficient 0.001, sampling temperature 1; each step has 32 questions and 16 responses per question, giving 512 responses per step; maximum response length is 32,768 tokens, and is relaxed to 65,536 after step 8,200, when both performance and response length jump noticeably. Training runs for 10,400 steps total, equivalent to going through the problem set 1.6 times.

sections.h: What it learned on its own

blocks.p: **First, performance rose sharply.** On AIME 2024, R1-Zero's average pass@1 climbed from 15.6% at the start of training to 77.9%. If each question is sampled multiple times and the majority answer is taken (self-consistency decoding), it reaches 86.7%, clearly above the average of human competitors. Broken down by difficulty, the hardest level of MATH questions went from about 0.55 to about 0.90.

**Second, it learned to "think longer" on its own.** During training, average response length rose steadily. In paper Figure 1(b), responses at the start are only one or two thousand tokens; later in training they pass 10,000. Nobody told it to write longer. This is entirely a result of reinforcement learning: thinking a little longer makes correct answers more likely, and correct answers bring reward.

**Third, reflection and checking emerged.** The paper invited three experts to list words that signal reflection: wait, mistake, however, verify, check, and others. During training, these words' occurrence increased to 5 to 7 times their initial frequency. The word "wait" is especially telling: almost absent early in training, it appears occasionally between steps 4,000 and 7,000, then surges after step 8,000.

The paper shows an intermediate model solving a radical equation and stopping midway: "Wait, wait. Here we can mark an aha moment. Let's recheck step by step..." Then it starts over with a different approach. The paper says this was also an "aha moment" for the research team itself.

callout.title: The model saying "wait" shows it is thinking like a human.
callout.text: The paper itself is cautious here. In the section on R1's cold-start data, it writes that users may find first-person, conversational reasoning more relatable, but this can invite unwarranted trust; these vivid reasoning patterns **mainly reflect heuristics designed by DeepSeek**, not evidence that the model has acquired human-like intelligence. The aha moment matters because reflection as a **behavior** was selected by reward, not taught by humans.

callout.title: Why rewarding only the result grows good process
callout.text: Imagine a student who receives only a right/wrong mark for each problem, with no explanation. Over time, they notice that writing too fast leads to mistakes, checking catches mistakes, and switching approaches when stuck often works. Nobody taught them to check, but the habit sticks because it raises their score. Reinforcement learning does exactly this, just at a scale of 512 answers per step and more than 10,000 steps. The precondition is that the student already has some foundation: if they cannot even read the problem, no amount of right/wrong feedback will help.

blocks.p: That foundation matters. The paper admits in the supplementary material that its initial attempts used a 7-billion-parameter dense model and a 16-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with pure RL, and saw **no clear improvement** on AIME: as soon as responses grew longer, they began to repeat. Only after switching to 32B, 230B, and 671B parameter models did pure RL show results. The paper also notes that DeepSeek-V3-Base's pretraining data contains a large amount of math and code, so the model has already "seen" many reasoning processes; reinforcement learning works by selecting and amplifying the good candidates among those it can already generate.

quiz.q: Did R1-Zero's reward include any scoring of the reasoning process itself?
options: Yes, a process reward model scored each step.
No, it only checked whether the final answer and the format were correct.
Yes, human annotators scored the reasoning process.
Yes, it rewarded longer responses.
quiz.why: The paper deliberately uses only rule-based rewards: whether the answer is correct and whether the format is correct. Longer responses and reflection are not directly required by the reward; they are byproducts of making correct answers more likely. The paper also avoids a process reward model because it is easy to game, as discussed later in the "failed attempts" section.

sections.h: From R1-Zero to R1: four stages

blocks.p: R1-Zero was strong at reasoning but had several problems: its outputs were hard to read, mixed Chinese and English (the base model was trained mainly on Chinese and English), and it had only been trained on reasoning tasks, so abilities such as writing and open-ended QA were limited. The final R1 uses a multi-stage pipeline to fix this:

fig.title: DeepSeek-R1 training pipeline
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: compiled from Figure 2, Section 3, and Supplementary B.3 of the paper. Dev1 through Dev3 are intermediate versions.

steps.name: Cold-start fine-tuning → Dev1
steps.desc: Use R1-Zero to generate solution processes, keep only the ones with correct answers and good formatting, then have humans and DeepSeek-V3 rewrite them into first-person, conversational, language-consistent style to fine-tune the base model.

steps.name: First RL round → Dev2
steps.desc: Train on reasoning problems as with R1-Zero, plus a reward for the proportion of target-language words in the chain of thought to prevent mixed Chinese-English.

steps.name: Rejection sampling + another fine-tuning → Dev3
steps.desc: Sample heavily from the previous model and keep only correct examples, producing about 600,000 reasoning examples; add about 200,000 non-reasoning examples in writing, QA, translation, and more, then fine-tune again from the base model.

steps.name: Second RL round → R1
steps.desc: Reasoning problems use rule-based rewards; general problems use helpfulness and harmlessness reward models. There are 1,700 steps total, and preference rewards are added only in the final 400 steps.

blocks.p: Several design choices worth noting:

list: **Cold start is about product experience**: the paper says it plainly—users find first-person thinking more intuitive and approachable. R1-Zero tends to use "we" or no pronoun; R1 more often uses "I."
**The language consistency reward has a cost**: an ablation showed that adding it left math performance largely unchanged while coding performance declined slightly. The paper chose readability.

**Preference rewards only in the final 400 steps**: the paper found that training with the reward model for too long leads to reward hacking: the helpfulness reward score kept rising while actual performance on reasoning problems declined.

**The helpfulness reward model looks only at the final summary**, ignoring the reasoning process to avoid interfering with it; **the harmlessness reward model looks at the whole response**, including the reasoning process. The former used 66,000 preference pairs; the latter used 106,000 responses labeled as safe/unsafe.
**The second RL round lowers the sampling temperature to 0.7.** The paper found that at this stage, too high a temperature generated incoherent content.

fig.title: What each stage contributed
fig.subtitle: From Table 3 of the paper. The blue column is the final R1.
fig.note: After cold start (Dev1), instruction following improves sharply, but AIME drops to 59.0, which the paper attributes to the small amount of cold-start data. The first RL round (Dev2) brings reasoning back; adding non-reasoning data (Dev3) fills in writing; the final RL round mainly improves general conversation.

sections.h: Results: matching o1, and "how long it thinks"

fig.title: R1 and representative models at the time
fig.subtitle: From Table 8 of the paper (selected metrics). o1-1217 results are from OpenAI's official report. The blue column is R1.
fig.note: On math and competitive programming, R1 roughly matches o1 and far exceeds non-reasoning models; on GPQA, which depends more on knowledge, R1 still trails o1. R1 and V3 are built on the same base model, so almost all of the gap comes from post-training.

blocks.p: To rule out the possibility that the problems had been seen during training, the paper also tested on AIME 2025, which was released after training: R1's pass@1 was 75%, and o1's was 80%. The paper concedes that its 10-gram decontamination method cannot catch paraphrased questions, and test sets released before 2024 may be contaminated.

**Reasoning models allocate "thinking time" by difficulty.** The paper tested 366 contest problems from 2024: R1 solved 61.8% and used an average of 8,793 thinking tokens per problem; easy problems took under 7,000, and the hardest took more than 18,000. For comparison, GPT-4o solved only 24.7% of the same problems and output an average of just 711 tokens.

Could a normal model close the gap by sampling more answers and voting? The paper says no: on AIME 2024, GPT-4o sampled 64 times and then voted, improving only from 9.3% to 13.4%. The reason is that those answers are independent of one another; none of them can look back, check, and correct itself. A reasoning model's advantage is that it can reflect and backtrack **within a single answer**.

sections.h: Distillation: the large model works it out, the small model learns it

blocks.p: The paper took the roughly 800,000 examples generated by R1, the same batch from stage three, and fine-tuned open-source Qwen and Llama models with supervised fine-tuning only, no reinforcement learning, producing six "distilled" models.

plain.title: The large model writes the solutions; the small model learns by following them.
plain.text: Have the reasoning-capable R1 write out complete thought processes for hundreds of thousands of problems. The small model then only needs to do ordinary supervised learning on these "standard answer plus process" examples—no RL of its own—to acquire decent reasoning. That is far cheaper than making a small model explore from scratch.

fig.title: The distilled small models
fig.subtitle: From Table 15 of the paper (selected). AIME 2024 and MATH-500 are pass@1.
fig.note: The 1.5-billion-parameter distilled model already beats GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet on math competition problems. Larger student models perform better.

blocks.p: Could a small model do its own reinforcement learning instead? The paper ran large-scale RL for more than 10,000 steps on a Qwen2.5-32B base model, reaching 47.0 on AIME 2024—comparable to QwQ-32B-Preview at the time (50.0)—while the same-size distilled version reached 72.6.

list: **Conclusion one**: distilling a strong model into a small model is cheap and effective. Having a small model run this paper's RL approach is computationally expensive and can still lose to distillation.
**Conclusion two**: distillation is economical, but pushing the frontier of human intelligence may still require stronger base models and larger-scale reinforcement learning.

callout.title: Distillation is "inheritance," not "discovery"
callout.text: Distillation lets a small model learn the ways of reasoning the large model already has, but new reasoning patterns are discovered in the large model's RL. This matches the earlier "foundation" finding: reinforcement learning amplifies capabilities the model already has—and the larger the model, the more there is to amplify.

fig.title: Compute cost of R1 post-training
fig.subtitle: From Supplementary Table 7 of the paper, estimated at a rental price of $2 per H800 GPU-hour.
fig.note: R1-Zero used 512 H800 GPUs for about 198 hours, and R1 used the same cards for about 80 hours. This is only the cost of post-training on top of DeepSeek-V3-Base; it does not include training the base model itself.

blocks.p: This figure is often compared with the hundreds of millions of dollars spent on large-model training, but it must be read carefully: it is only the cost of the "reasoning layer" added on top. The paper is not claiming that a few hundred thousand dollars can produce R1. It is saying that, on top of a sufficiently strong base model, prompting reasoning through reinforcement learning does not require an astronomical budget.

The paper includes a section titled "attempts that did not work" and stresses that this does not mean those methods are necessarily invalid. It is very helpful for understanding why R1 ended up the way it did.

list: **Process reward model (PRM)**: scoring each step of reasoning sounds more reasonable than scoring only the result. In practice it has three problems. In general reasoning, it is hard to define what counts as a "step." Judging whether an intermediate step is correct is itself hard: model annotations are unreliable, and human annotation cannot be done at scale. Once model scoring is introduced, reward hacking appears. The paper concludes that PRMs can be useful for reranking candidate answers, but in large-scale RL they are not worth the cost.

**Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS)**: inspired by AlphaGo, it breaks an answer into small steps and searches systematically through the solution space. The difficulty is that the search space in a board game is relatively well-defined, while the search space for text generation is exponential. Restricting how many children each node can expand easily leads to local optima, and the value model needed to guide the search is hard to train. So the model cannot improve through self-play the way AlphaGo does.

blocks.p: Both failures point to the same conclusion: **intermediate steps are hard to score reliably**. R1's success comes precisely from sidestepping this problem: it scores only the final result, and leaves the question of how to get there entirely to the model's own exploration.

list: **That "25% improvement" is in percentage points**: the main text says the final stage improved AlpacaEval 2.0 by 25% and ArenaHard by 17%. Checking Table 3, the former went from 62.1 to 87.6 and the latter from 75.6 to 92.3—those are absolute differences, in percentage points. As relative increases, they are about 41% and 22%.

**"4 days, about 80 hours"**: the supplementary material says R1 training took "about 4 days, about 80 hours." Four days is 96 hours; dividing the 41,000 GPU-hours in Table 7 by 512 GPUs gives about 80 hours, so 80 is the number that checks out.

**Take the IF-Eval claim with a grain of salt**: the main text calls R1's IF-Eval performance "impressive," but in Table 8, R1 is 83.3, below DeepSeek-V3's 86.1 and Claude 3.5 Sonnet's 86.5. It is, however, a large jump from R1-Zero's 46.6.

**The clipping range is set very large**: in the first RL stage, GRPO's clipping parameter ε is set to 10, far larger than in typical PPO settings. The paper says that too small a clipping range truncates the gradients of many tokens and hurts performance, while too large becomes unstable. The author contributions also note that the team specifically proposed this "large clipping" strategy.

**The base model is not completely "clean"**: the paper concedes that the pretraining web pages for V3-Base contain many answers generated by OpenAI models, so the base model may have indirectly learned knowledge from other strong models. But the team did not deliberately add OpenAI-generated synthetic data at the end of pretraining.

sections.h: Limitations, and the end of Path 1

blocks.p: The paper lists these limitations:

list: **Structured output and tool use**: it cannot yet call tools such as a search engine or a calculator.
**Token efficiency**: it may think too long on simple questions.
**Language mixing**: it is optimized only for Chinese and English; questions in other languages may be thought through and answered in English.
**Prompt sensitivity**: few-shot prompts degrade performance; the paper recommends describing the problem directly and using zero-shot.
**Software engineering**: evaluation was too slow to run RL at scale, so improvement over V3 is limited.

**Reward hacking**: pure RL relies on reliable rewards. For tasks such as writing, where rules cannot determine correctness, the reward must come from a model, and the longer training runs, the easier it is to game. These tasks currently still rely on human-labeled supervised data, with RL run for only a few hundred steps.

blocks.p: The paper's outlook is bold: for any task that a verifier can judge effectively, no matter how difficult for humans, machines trained this way may surpass humans. The real difficulty is tasks for which reliable rewards are hard to construct.

**What happened next.** After R1 was open-sourced, GRPO and "RL with verifiable rewards" quickly became a standard approach for training reasoning models, and the community produced many reproductions and improvements. In September 2025, the paper was published in Nature, making it one of the earlier large-language-model papers to pass peer review.

sections.h: Check yourself: did you really get it?

quiz.q: When training with GRPO, if all 16 responses to a question are correct, what does that question contribute to the model update?
options: The largest contribution, because the reward is highest.
Almost none: the rewards in the group are identical, so after subtracting the mean the advantage is 0.
It makes the model worse.
It is automatically replaced with a harder question.
quiz.why: Advantage is "how much better than the group average." When every answer is correct, everyone is average, so there is no better response and the question provides no learning signal. The same applies when every answer is wrong. This is why training questions need to be at the right difficulty: the model has to be sometimes right and sometimes wrong to learn anything.

quiz.q: Why did R1's second RL stage add preference rewards only in the final 400 steps?
options: To save compute.
The paper found that training with the reward model for too long leads to reward hacking: reward scores rise while actual reasoning performance drops.
Because the preference data only had 400 examples.
Because the earlier steps were used for distillation.
quiz.why: A reward model is only an approximation of human preference. The longer the model trains, the more likely it is to find shortcuts that fool the reward. Rule-based rewards—whether the answer is correct—cannot be gamed, so the reasoning portion can train for a long time. The portion scored by a model can only train briefly.

quiz.q: What did the paper's experiments show about distillation versus reinforcement learning?
options: RL on a small model is always better than distillation.
For a 32-billion-parameter model, distilling from R1 clearly outperforms doing large-scale RL on its own.
All distilled models used RL.
Distillation only works for Llama.
quiz.why: Qwen2.5-32B doing its own RL for more than 10,000 steps reached only 47.0 on AIME; the same-size model distilled from R1 reached 72.6. Using RL to discover new reasoning patterns requires a powerful base model. Smaller models are better off simply inheriting.

blocks.p: After reading this, you should be able to answer these questions:

list: Why is reasoning a good fit for reinforcement learning, while preference alignment can be handled with DPO?
How does GRPO compute advantage, and why does it not need a value model?
How does GRPO's KL penalty differ from PPO's, and why does that matter for long chain-of-thought?
What makes up R1-Zero's reward, and why does it avoid neural reward models?
What does the 'aha moment' show, and what does it not show?
What does each of R1's four stages solve?
Why does base model scale matter so much for pure reinforcement learning?
Why didn't the process reward model and Monte Carlo tree search work?
